messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amira was twenty-eight when the afternoon harvest in the valley turned to chaos. She had been sorting crates near the edge of the packing facility when a violent altercation erupted between two families over a disputed water supply. What struck her most was not just the sudden shift in the air, but the way the crowd’s eyes narrowed into suspicious, scanning gazes, the sharp exclamations about safety and betrayal, and the high, desperate wail of an infant caught in the crush. Amira froze, her hands trembling as she watched strangers turn on one another in seconds, her nervous system imprinting the exact sequence of panic, the language of fear, and the sound of crying children. In the months that followed, those moments never truly left her. The memory lived in her body as a tightness in her chest whenever the subject of community disputes or personal safety came up over dinner. If someone’s posture grew rigid or their eyes darted away in the checkout line, her breath would catch, instantly pulling her back to the crush of the packing lot. Those flashes did not merely remind her of the violence; they convinced her that people were fundamentally unpredictable and untrustworthy, that the ground beneath her feet was inherently unstable. Slowly, her confidence in the world and in any higher order of things eroded. She began to feel she no longer belonged anywhere, as if the safety she had once taken for granted was a myth. In the orchards where she now worked as an agricultural laborer, these feelings took root in her daily routine. When a foreman’s raised voice or a coworker’s sideways glance felt too close to that old panic, Amira would excuse herself to the toolshed. She would scrub her hands until the skin reddened, meticulously aligning every trowel and pruner by size, believing that if she could just impose perfect order on her surroundings, the world would finally make sense. She told herself to focus on the beauty of the blooming trees, forcing a smile when her thoughts grew dark, and when the images of the crowd surged forward, she would deliberately push them down, clenching her jaw and repeating a single reassuring phrase in her head. Yet her growing conviction that the world was inherently unsafe and that she was fundamentally alone drove these rituals deeper into her routine. Because she had lost faith in any higher protection and distrusted the intentions of those around her, Amira felt she could only rely on rigid, personal control. She extended the compulsive organizing from the toolshed to her own divorced and now empty apartment, arranging kitchenware in precise rows and wiping the same counters until dawn, convinced that if she could just engineer enough order, she might finally feel safe. She continued forcing positive narratives over the intrusions and actively suppressing the memories, not because they had faded, but because her appraisals told her that surrendering to the pain was simply too dangerous. Her recent screening had registered a sixty-five on the PCL-5, mirroring the relentless tightness in her chest and the way her nervous system remained permanently primed. The strategies only widened the distance between her and the present. The forced positivity felt like a thin veneer over a fault line, making every subsequent conversation about safety or community feel like a trap she couldn’t escape. Her compulsive organizing offered no relief once she returned to the fields; the neatly stacked tools could not stop her from scanning the horizon for threats, and the harder she tried to suppress the intrusions, the more violently they resurfaced. Over time, the futility of her control became proof that she was fundamentally unsafe. She stopped attending the worker breaks, citing headaches and tiredness, until her supervisors noted her declining pace and her inability to collaborate on the harvest quotas. The isolation deepened her conviction that she was an outsider in her own life, reinforcing the very appraisals she had tried to outrun. The breaking point arrived on a late summer evening when a nearby neighborhood baby monitor crackled through an open window, the cry sharp and unfamiliar. Amira collapsed against the wall, her hands shaking so badly she could not even reach for her keys. What finally drove her to the clinic was not the fear of the sound itself, but the terrifying realization that her own efforts to stay safe had only built a prison around her. She sat in the waiting room now, hoping the therapist could help her untangle the knot of dread without forcing her to face the violence again, terrified that the ground would give way beneath her once more.
